claim: In vestibular cerebellum, primary afferents carry signals from single vestibular end organs.
source: In vestibular cerebellum, primary afferents carry signals from single vestibular end organs, whereas secondary afferents from vestibular nucleus carry integrated signals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational claim about the vestibular cerebellar circuit.

claim: Secondary afferents from vestibular nucleus carry integrated signals.
source: In vestibular cerebellum, primary afferents carry signals from single vestibular end organs, whereas secondary afferents from vestibular nucleus carry integrated signals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational claim about the vestibular cerebellar circuit.

claim: ON UBCs transform single mossy fiber signals into long-lasting excitation.
source: We focused on vestibular projections to ON and OFF classes of unipolar brush cells (UBCs), which transform single mossy fiber signals into long-lasting excitation or inhibition respectively, and impact the activity of ensembles of granule cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the functional properties of ON UBCs.

claim: OFF UBCs transform single mossy fiber signals into long-lasting inhibition.
source: We focused on vestibular projections to ON and OFF classes of unipolar brush cells (UBCs), which transform single mossy fiber signals into long-lasting excitation or inhibition respectively, and impact the activity of ensembles of granule cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the functional properties of OFF UBCs.

claim: UBCs impact the activity of ensembles of granule cells.
source: We focused on vestibular projections to ON and OFF classes of unipolar brush cells (UBCs), which transform single mossy fiber signals into long-lasting excitation or inhibition respectively, and impact the activity of ensembles of granule cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the downstream effects of UBCs.

claim: A specialized subset of primary afferents contacts ON UBCs, but not OFF UBCs.
source: We show that a specialized subset of primary afferents contacts ON UBCs, but not OFF UBCs, while secondary afferents contact both subtypes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by physiological and anatomical data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Secondary afferents contact both ON and OFF UBC subtypes.
source: We show that a specialized subset of primary afferents contacts ON UBCs, but not OFF UBCs, while secondary afferents contact both subtypes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by physiological and anatomical data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Striking anatomical differences were observed between primary and secondary afferents.
source: Striking anatomical differences were observed between primary and secondary afferents, their synapses, and the UBCs they contact.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by morphological measurements and imaging data in the manuscript.

claim: Striking anatomical differences were observed between the synapses of primary and secondary afferents.
source: Striking anatomical differences were observed between primary and secondary afferents, their synapses, and the UBCs they contact.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by morphological measurements and imaging data in the manuscript.

claim: Striking anatomical differences were observed between the UBCs contacted by primary and secondary afferents.
source: Striking anatomical differences were observed between primary and secondary afferents, their synapses, and the UBCs they contact.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by morphological measurements and imaging data in the manuscript.

claim: Each class of UBC functions to transform specific signals through distinct anatomical pathways.
source: Thus, each class of UBC functions to transform specific signals through distinct anatomical pathways.
evidence: This is the concluding statement of the abstract, synthesizing the findings of the study.

claim: Mossy fibers in the cerebellum convey multimodal signals from diverse regions of the central nervous system to the granule cell layer.
source: In the cerebellum, mossy fibers convey multimodal signals from diverse regions of the central nervous system to the granule cell layer.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: 'Expansion recoding' theories of cerebellar processing require mossy fiber inputs to diverge to hundreds of granule cells.
source: 'Expansion recoding' theories of cerebellar processing require these mossy fiber inputs to diverge to hundreds of granule cells, and their signals are integrated first by granule cell dendrites and then by the massive dendritic trees of Purkinje cells (Albus, 1971).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical framework with citation to Albus, 1971.

claim: Mossy fiber signals are integrated first by granule cell dendrites and then by the massive dendritic trees of Purkinje cells.
source: 'Expansion recoding' theories of cerebellar processing require these mossy fiber inputs to diverge to hundreds of granule cells, and their signals are integrated first by granule cell dendrites and then by the massive dendritic trees of Purkinje cells (Albus, 1971).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical framework with citation to Albus, 1971.

claim: Mossy fiber inputs to vestibular cerebellum differ from those of other cerebellar lobes in receiving mossy fibers directly from peripheral ganglion neurons (the primary vestibular afferents).
source: However, mossy fiber inputs to vestibular cerebellum differ from those of other cerebellar lobes in receiving mossy fibers directly from peripheral ganglion neurons (the primary vestibular afferents), as well as from brainstem nuclei (secondary afferents).
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of the vestibular cerebellum.

claim: Mossy fiber inputs to vestibular cerebellum receive mossy fibers from brainstem nuclei (secondary afferents).
source: However, mossy fiber inputs to vestibular cerebellum differ from those of other cerebellar lobes in receiving mossy fibers directly from peripheral ganglion neurons (the primary vestibular afferents), as well as from brainstem nuclei (secondary afferents).
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of the vestibular cerebellum.

claim: Each of the primary afferents carries signals from a single vestibular organ.
source: Each of the primary afferents carries signals from a single vestibular organ, with each organ coding head position or velocity in a given plane (Fernández et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Fernández et al., 1988.

claim: Each vestibular organ codes head position or velocity in a given plane.
source: Each of the primary afferents carries signals from a single vestibular organ, with each organ coding head position or velocity in a given plane (Fernández et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Fernández et al., 1988.

claim: UBCs are excitatory interneurons within the granule cell layer.
source: UBCs are excitatory interneurons within the granule cell layer that receive a single mossy fiber ending on their brush-like dendrite (Harris et al., 1993; Mugnaini and Floris, 1994; Mugnaini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Harris et al., 1993; Mugnaini and Floris, 1994; Mugnaini et al., 2011.

claim: UBCs receive a single mossy fiber ending on their brush-like dendrite.
source: UBCs are excitatory interneurons within the granule cell layer that receive a single mossy fiber ending on their brush-like dendrite (Harris et al., 1993; Mugnaini and Floris, 1994; Mugnaini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Harris et al., 1993; Mugnaini and Floris, 1994; Mugnaini et al., 2011.

claim: The large synaptic contact between mossy fiber and UBC dramatically transforms activity of one mossy fiber before projecting to hundreds of granule cells and other UBCs.
source: Instead of integrating multiple inputs as granule cells do, this large synaptic contact dramatically transforms activity of one mossy fiber before projecting to hundreds of granule cells and other UBCs.
evidence: This is stated as a functional characteristic of UBCs.

claim: UBCs are present in exceptionally high density in vestibular processing areas of rodent cerebellum.
source: In vestibular processing areas of rodent cerebellum, UBCs are present in exceptionally high density and could coordinate ensembles of granule cells to respond to single directions of movement (Floris et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Floris et al., 1994.

claim: UBCs could coordinate ensembles of granule cells to respond to single directions of movement.
source: In vestibular processing areas of rodent cerebellum, UBCs are present in exceptionally high density and could coordinate ensembles of granule cells to respond to single directions of movement (Floris et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with citation to Floris et al., 1994.

claim: Two subtypes of UBC have been described: ON UBCs and OFF UBCs.
source: Two subtypes of UBC have been described: ON UBCs respond to mossy fiber input with a prolonged depolarization and enhancement of firing while OFF UBCs are inhibited (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015.

claim: ON UBCs respond to mossy fiber input with a prolonged depolarization and enhancement of firing.
source: Two subtypes of UBC have been described: ON UBCs respond to mossy fiber input with a prolonged depolarization and enhancement of firing while OFF UBCs are inhibited (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015.

claim: OFF UBCs are inhibited in response to mossy fiber input.
source: Two subtypes of UBC have been described: ON UBCs respond to mossy fiber input with a prolonged depolarization and enhancement of firing while OFF UBCs are inhibited (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015.

claim: Both ON and OFF UBC responses last for hundreds of milliseconds.
source: Both responses last for hundreds of milliseconds, an outcome of selective receptor expression in the two subtypes (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015) combined with the great size the mossy fiber-UBC synaptic contact (Mugnaini et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015 and Mugnaini et al., 1994.

claim: The prolonged responses of ON and OFF UBCs are an outcome of selective receptor expression in the two subtypes.
source: Both responses last for hundreds of milliseconds, an outcome of selective receptor expression in the two subtypes (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015) combined with the great size the mossy fiber-UBC synaptic contact (Mugnaini et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015.

claim: The prolonged responses of ON and OFF UBCs are an outcome of the great size of the mossy fiber-UBC synaptic contact.
source: Both responses last for hundreds of milliseconds, an outcome of selective receptor expression in the two subtypes (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015) combined with the great size the mossy fiber-UBC synaptic contact (Mugnaini et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Mugnaini et al., 1994.

claim: In cerebellar lobe X of mouse, the primary representation is from a subset of angular acceleration coding neurons.
source: Here we show that in cerebellar lobe X of mouse, the primary representation is from a subset of angular acceleration coding neurons, and these signals reach and are amplified by ON UBCs, but not OFF UBCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Primary vestibular signals reach and are amplified by ON UBCs, but not OFF UBCs.
source: Here we show that in cerebellar lobe X of mouse, the primary representation is from a subset of angular acceleration coding neurons, and these signals reach and are amplified by ON UBCs, but not OFF UBCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: OFF UBCs only process secondary afferent signals that may contain signals integrated over multiple directions of movement, hemispheres and/or modalities.
source: OFF UBCs by contrast only process secondary afferent signals that may contain signals integrated over multiple directions of movement, hemispheres and/or modalities.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Primary and secondary inputs exhibit dramatic differences in their axonal morphology.
source: We also show that primary and secondary inputs exhibit dramatic differences in their axonal and synaptic morphology, as well as in the morphology of the UBCs they contact, which may further refine coding in the granule cell layer.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by morphological data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Primary and secondary inputs exhibit dramatic differences in their synaptic morphology.
source: We also show that primary and secondary inputs exhibit dramatic differences in their axonal and synaptic morphology, as well as in the morphology of the UBCs they contact, which may further refine coding in the granule cell layer.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by morphological data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Primary and secondary inputs exhibit dramatic differences in the morphology of the UBCs they contact.
source: We also show that primary and secondary inputs exhibit dramatic differences in their axonal and synaptic morphology, as well as in the morphology of the UBCs they contact, which may further refine coding in the granule cell layer.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by morphological data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The morphological differences between primary and secondary inputs may further refine coding in the granule cell layer.
source: We also show that primary and secondary inputs exhibit dramatic differences in their axonal and synaptic morphology, as well as in the morphology of the UBCs they contact, which may further refine coding in the granule cell layer.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the observed morphological differences.

claim: The Glt25d2 mouse line expresses Cre in primary afferents projecting to the vestibular nuclei and vestibular lobes of the cerebellum.
source: In order to express transgenes in primary afferents that may project to UBCs in the vestibular cerebellum, we determined that the Glt25d2 mouse line that has Cre recombinase (Cre) targeted to the Colgalt2 locus (B6-Tg(Colgalt2-cre)NF107Gsat) (Gerfen et al., 2013) expresses Cre in primary afferents projecting to the vestibular nuclei and vestibular lobes of the cerebellum, by crossing it with a tdTomato reporter line (Ai9) (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by Figure 1A-B showing tdTomato expression in primary afferents.

claim: In cerebellar lobes IX and X, Glt25d2-labeled afferents appeared as mossy fibers and were most likely primary (first-order) from the VG.
source: In cerebellar lobes IX and X, these afferents appeared as mossy fibers, and were most likely primary (first-order) from the VG, and not those from brainstem vestibular nuclei or nucleus prepositus hypoglossi that also project to cerebellum, because no somata lying in these areas expressed Cre (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the absence of Cre-expressing somata in brainstem nuclei, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: Primary afferents did not project to flocculus or paraflocculus.
source: Primary afferents did not project to flocculus or paraflocculus.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the Glt25d2 mouse line.

claim: VG neurons have specialized dendrites that receive input from vestibular hair cells in the five vestibular end organs: the three semicircular canals and the two otolith organs, the utricle and sacculus.
source: VG neurons have specialized dendrites that receive input from vestibular hair cells in the five vestibular end organs: the three semicircular canals and the two otolith organs, the utricle and sacculus.
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge.

claim: There are 3 types of peripheral afferent neuron based on their dendritic morphology: 'pure-calyx', bouton, and dimorphic.
source: There are 3 types of peripheral afferent neuron based on their dendritic morphology: 'pure-calyx', which form calyx endings on Type I hair cells, bouton, which makes bouton endings on Type II hair cells, and dimorphic, which have both calyx and bouton terminals (Fernández et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Fernández et al., 1988.

claim: 'Pure-calyx' afferents form calyx endings on Type I hair cells.
source: There are 3 types of peripheral afferent neuron based on their dendritic morphology: 'pure-calyx', which form calyx endings on Type I hair cells, bouton, which makes bouton endings on Type II hair cells, and dimorphic, which have both calyx and bouton terminals (Fernández et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Fernández et al., 1988.

claim: Bouton afferents make bouton endings on Type II hair cells.
source: There are 3 types of peripheral afferent neuron based on their dendritic morphology: 'pure-calyx', which form calyx endings on Type I hair cells, bouton, which makes bouton endings on Type II hair cells, and dimorphic, which have both calyx and bouton terminals (Fernández et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Fernández et al., 1988.

claim: Dimorphic afferents have both calyx and bouton terminals.
source: There are 3 types of peripheral afferent neuron based on their dendritic morphology: 'pure-calyx', which form calyx endings on Type I hair cells, bouton, which makes bouton endings on Type II hair cells, and dimorphic, which have both calyx and bouton terminals (Fernández et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Fernández et al., 1988.

claim: The central regions of each end-organ are populated with 'pure-calyx' type dendritic endings of VG neurons expressing calretinin.
source: The central regions of each end-organ are populated with 'pure-calyx' type dendritic endings of VG neurons expressing calretinin (Desmadryl and Dechesne, 1992; Leonard and Kevetter, 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Desmadryl and Dechesne, 1992; Leonard and Kevetter, 2002.

claim: Pure-calyx endings also receive input from Type II hair cells that contact the outer surface of the calyx.
source: Note that pure-calyx endings also receive input from Type II hair cells that contact the outer surface of the calyx.
evidence: This is stated as a clarification about the connectivity of pure-calyx endings.

claim: tdTomato-positive VG neurons in the Glt25d2::tdTomato mouse varied in soma size, location and calretinin expression.
source: tdTomato-positive VG neurons in the Glt25d2::tdTomato mouse varied in soma size, location and calretinin expression (Figure 1D–E), indicating Cre expression in diverse types of VG neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 1D-E.

claim: Cre expression in the Glt25d2 mouse line occurs in diverse types of VG neurons.
source: tdTomato-positive VG neurons in the Glt25d2::tdTomato mouse varied in soma size, location and calretinin expression (Figure 1D–E), indicating Cre expression in diverse types of VG neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the variability in soma size, location, and calretinin expression, supported by Figure 1D-E.

claim: Some peripheral afferents that expressed tdTomato had pure-calyx endings.
source: Indeed, some peripheral afferents that expressed tdTomato had pure-calyx endings (based on co-labeling with calretinin) and others had dimorphic endings (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 1F-G.

claim: Some peripheral afferents that expressed tdTomato had dimorphic endings.
source: Indeed, some peripheral afferents that expressed tdTomato had pure-calyx endings (based on co-labeling with calretinin) and others had dimorphic endings (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 1F-G.

claim: Retro-AAVs infect axons and allow the source of projections to the injected site to be determined.
source: To determine which signals are carried to cerebellum via Cre+ primary afferents in the Glt25d2 mouse line, we used retrogradely-infecting adeno-associated viruses (retro-AAVs) that express GFP. Unlike typical AAVs, retro-AAVs infect axons and thus allow the source of projections to the injected site to be determined (Tervo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Tervo et al., 2016.

claim: In a total of 670 retrolabeled VG somata, none expressed calretinin.
source: In a total of 670 retrolabeled VG somata, none expressed calretinin (n = 5 ganglia in separate experiments), suggesting that Cre-positive (Cre+) cells with pure-calyx endings do not project to lobe X.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: Cre-positive cells with pure-calyx endings do not project to lobe X.
source: In a total of 670 retrolabeled VG somata, none expressed calretinin (n = 5 ganglia in separate experiments), suggesting that Cre-positive (Cre+) cells with pure-calyx endings do not project to lobe X.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the absence of calretinin expression in retrolabeled VG somata.

claim: The afferents in the end organs were almost exclusively dimorphic, having calyx endings surrounding hair cells with extending processes ending in boutons.
source: The afferents in the end organs were almost exclusively dimorphic, having calyx endings surrounding hair cells with extending processes ending in boutons (Figure 2D–H).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from retrograde tracing experiments, supported by Figure 2D-H.

claim: No pure-calyx endings and only one bouton-only ending was observed in retrolabeled afferents.
source: No pure-calyx endings and only one bouton-only ending was observed (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative observation from retrograde tracing experiments, supported by Figure 2C.

claim: No retrolabeled afferents were co-labeled with calretinin (0 of 380 calyces, two mice, 10 end organs).
source: No retrolabeled afferents were co-labeled with calretinin (0 of 380 calyces, two mice, 10 end organs), consistent with the counts of labeled VG somata.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: Most of the retrolabeled afferents surrounded hair cells in the semicircular canals and the sacculus.
source: Most of the retrolabeled afferents surrounded hair cells in the semicircular canals and the sacculus (anterior canal, 55, 64; horizontal canal, 22, 35; posterior vertical canal, 55, 50; utricle, 5, 6; sacculus; 53, 35; numbers are retrolabeled calyces in each experiment where injections were restricted to lobe X).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: The source of Cre+ primary vestibular afferents that project to lobe X are mostly dimorphic afferents in the ipsilateral semicircular canals and extrastriolar regions of the sacculus.
source: In sum, in the Glt25d2 mouse line the source of Cre+ primary vestibular afferents that project to lobe X are mostly dimorphic afferents in the ipsilateral semicircular canals and extrastriolar regions of the sacculus, and are therefore likely to predominantly convey information about angular acceleration of the head.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the retrograde tracing findings.

claim: Cre+ primary vestibular afferents that project to lobe X are likely to predominantly convey information about angular acceleration of the head.
source: In sum, in the Glt25d2 mouse line the source of Cre+ primary vestibular afferents that project to lobe X are mostly dimorphic afferents in the ipsilateral semicircular canals and extrastriolar regions of the sacculus, and are therefore likely to predominantly convey information about angular acceleration of the head.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the anatomical origin of the afferents.

claim: 2.7% of retrogradely labeled VG somata were calretinin-positive when using non-Cre-dependent retrograde virus targeting lobe X.
source: VG ipsilateral to the site of injection had many retrogradely labeled somata, including 2.7% that were calretinin-positive (34/1486, n = 3 VG in separate experiments).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from retrograde tracing experiments using non-Cre-dependent virus.

claim: The majority of calretinin positive cells were not retrolabeled (91%, 343/377) when using non-Cre-dependent retrograde virus targeting lobe X.
source: The majority of calretinin positive cells were not retrolabeled (91%, 343/377).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from retrograde tracing experiments using non-Cre-dependent virus.

claim: Examples of central/striolar pure-calyx afferents that were retrolabeled were found in all five end organs, although they were rare.
source: Examples of central/striolar pure-calyx afferents that were retrolabeled were found in all five end organs, although they were rare, numbering only a few per end organ (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from retrograde tracing experiments using non-Cre-dependent virus, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Some pure-calyx afferents may project to cerebellum, but it cannot be determined whether they project to lobe X, lobe IX or cerebellar nuclei.
source: This provides evidence that some pure-calyx afferents may project to cerebellum, but we cannot determine whether they project to lobe X, lobe IX or cerebellar nuclei, as all regions were infected.
evidence: This is stated as an inference with limitations based on the retrograde tracing experiments using non-Cre-dependent virus.

claim: All 13 UBCs that responded to optogenetic activation of primary afferents were ON UBCs.
source: However, of 107 UBCs recorded in brain slices from 22 mice, all 13 UBCs that responded to optogenetic activation of primary afferents were ON UBCs.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The response to ChR2 stimulation of primary afferents was remarkably similar to responses evoked by electrical stimulation of white matter.
source: The response to ChR2 stimulation of primary afferents was remarkably similar to responses evoked by electrical stimulation of white matter (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 3D.

claim: Primary afferents preferentially target ON UBCs and we found no evidence for primary projections to OFF UBCs.
source: Thus, primary afferents preferentially target ON UBCs and we found no evidence for primary projections to OFF UBCs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The area of the brush that contacted the mossy fiber was 99.45 ± 40.95 µm2 (mean ± SD).
source: The area of the brush that contacted the mossy fiber was 99.45 ± 40.95 µm2 (mean ± SD).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative measurement from 3D reconstructions of biocytin-filled cells.

claim: The area of the UBC brush itself was 446.68 ± 86.35 µm2 (mean ± SD).
source: The area of the UBC brush itself was 446.68 ± 86.35 µm2 (mean ± SD), and thus nearly a quarter of the dendrite was available for synaptic contact.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative measurement from 3D reconstructions of biocytin-filled cells.

claim: Nearly a quarter of the UBC dendrite was available for synaptic contact.
source: The area of the UBC brush itself was 446.68 ± 86.35 µm2 (mean ± SD), and thus nearly a quarter of the dendrite was available for synaptic contact.
evidence: This is stated as a calculation based on the measured brush and contact areas.

claim: The postsynaptic fast EPSC was positively correlated with UBC brush area, but not the contact area between the mossy fiber and brush.
source: The postsynaptic fast EPSC was positively correlated with UBC brush area, but not the contact area between the mossy fiber and brush (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from correlation analysis, supported by Figure 3I.

claim: The slow EPSC amplitudes that occur at the offset of stimulation and decay times did not correlate with the contact area between the mossy fiber and UBC or the brush area.
source: The slow EPSC amplitudes that occur at the offset of stimulation and decay times did not correlate with the contact area between the mossy fiber and UBC or the brush area (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from correlation analysis, supported by Figure 3J.

claim: The lack of correlation between slow EPSC and contact area may suggest that the postsynaptic AMPARs that mediate this slow current are at some distance from the sites of contact with the mossy fiber, or that glutamate removal by diffusion or transport shape this current.
source: This lack of correlation may suggest that the postsynaptic AMPARs that mediate this slow current are at some distance from the sites of contact with the mossy fiber, or that glutamate removal by diffusion or transport shape this current (Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis to explain the lack of correlation, with citation to Lu et al., 2017.

claim: mGluR1 is expressed by ON UBCs and not by OFF UBCs.
source: mGluR1 is expressed by ON UBCs and not by OFF UBCs, while calretinin is expressed by OFF UBCs and not by ON UBCs (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015.

claim: Calretinin is expressed by OFF UBCs and not by ON UBCs.
source: mGluR1 is expressed by ON UBCs and not by OFF UBCs, while calretinin is expressed by OFF UBCs and not by ON UBCs (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015.

claim: Immunohistochemical labeling revealed numerous projections to mGluR1-expressing UBCs, but not to calretinin-expressing UBCs.
source: Immunohistochemical labeling of these two markers of UBC subtype in cerebellar sections of Glt25d2::tdTomato mice expressing tdTomato in primary afferents revealed numerous projections to mGluR1-expressing UBCs, but not to calretinin-expressing UBCs (Figure 3K–M), confirming the physiological analysis.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from immunohistochemistry, supported by Figure 3K-M.

claim: 20% of mGluR1-expressing UBCs received primary afferent input.
source: Overall 145 mGluR1-expressing UBCs were counted, 29 of which received primary afferent input (20%).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from systematic sampling of lobe X.

claim: None of the 96 calretinin+ UBCs counted received primary afferent input.
source: In the same brain sections 96 calretinin+ UBCs were counted, none of which received primary afferent input.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from systematic sampling of lobe X.

claim: A direct VG projection to lobe X targets mGluR1-expressing ON UBCs but not calretinin-expressing OFF UBCs.
source: Thus, a direct VG projection to lobe X targets mGluR1-expressing ON UBCs but not calretinin-expressing OFF UBCs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the immunohistochemistry and systematic sampling experiments.

claim: Of the VG neurons infected by viral injection into the posterior semicircular canal, ~8.4% expressed calretinin and were therefore the 'pure-calyx' type.
source: Of the VG neurons infected, ~8.4% expressed calretinin and were therefore the 'pure-calyx' type (Out of 636 virus labeled neurons in 4 VG, 54 expressed calretinin).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from viral labeling experiments.

claim: Of the 240 mossy fiber terminals imaged, 79 mGluR1-expressing UBCs had brushes interdigitated with the terminals.
source: Of the 240 mossy fiber terminals imaged, 79 mGluR1-expressing UBCs had brushes interdigitated with the terminals (n = 4 mice).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from viral labeling and imaging experiments.

claim: No calretinin-expressing UBCs were seen making contact to primary vestibular afferents labeled by viral injection into the posterior semicircular canal.
source: No calretinin-expressing UBCs were seen making contact to primary vestibular afferents.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from viral labeling and imaging experiments.

claim: Primary vestibular afferents seldom branched as they projected along the white matter in the sagittal plane.
source: The morphology of the primary afferents was striking. They seldom branched as they projected along the white matter in the sagittal plane.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from viral labeling and imaging experiments.

claim: Primary vestibular afferents project exclusively to mGluR1-expressing ON UBCs and not to calretinin-expressing OFF UBCs.
source: Taken together, these data provide multiple lines of evidence showing that primary vestibular afferents project exclusively to mGluR1-expressing ON UBCs and not to calretinin-expressing OFF UBCs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Some UBCs that received direct primary afferents had ChR2-evoked fast disynaptic inhibitory post synaptic currents (IPSCs) in addition to monosynaptic EPSCs.
source: Indeed, some UBCs that received direct primary afferents had ChR2-evoked fast disynaptic inhibitory post synaptic currents (IPSCs) in addition to monosynaptic EPSCs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The onset of disynaptic IPSCs occurred at a delay consistent with disynaptic inhibition in all cases (5.74 ± 1.42 ms (mean ± SD), n = 23).
source: The onset of these IPSCs occurred at a delay consistent with disynaptic inhibition in all cases (5.74 ± 1.42 ms (mean ± SD), n = 23).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: In most UBCs, some component of the IPSC was blocked by GABAAR antagonist SR-95531 and the remaining current was blocked by glycine receptor antagonist strychnine.
source: In most of these UBCs some component of the IPSC was blocked by GABAAR antagonist SR-95531 and the remaining current was blocked by glycine receptor antagonist strychnine (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from pharmacology experiments, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Cerebellar Golgi cells, which co-release GABA and glycine, are presumably the source of disynaptic inhibition.
source: Presumably cerebellar Golgi cells, which co-release GABA and glycine, are the source of this disynaptic inhibition (Rousseau et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as an inference with citation to Rousseau et al., 2012.

claim: The same population of primary vestibular afferents both excite ON UBCs and activate a pathway that leads to their inhibition.
source: Thus, the same population of primary vestibular afferents both excite ON UBCs and activate a pathway that leads to their inhibition.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the electrophysiology experiments showing both excitation and disynaptic inhibition.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Cre+ afferents resulted in fast EPSCs in granule cells, but never exhibited a slow AMPAR-mediated EPSC at the offset of stimulation.
source: Optogenetic activation of Cre+ afferents resulted in fast EPSCs in granule cells, but never exhibited a slow AMPAR-mediated EPSC at the offset of stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from electrophysiology experiments, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The contact area between mossy fiber and granule cell claw was only about 15% of those measured between primary afferent and UBC brush.
source: The contact area between mossy fiber and granule cell claw was only about 15% of those measured between primary afferent and UBC brush (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C–K).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from morphological measurements, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 4C-K.

claim: The slow EPSC of UBCs results from pre and postsynaptic structure, and is not simply a feature of mossy fiber transmitter release per se.
source: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that the slow EPSC of UBCs results from pre and postsynaptic structure, and is not simply a feature of mossy fiber transmitter release per se.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the comparison of UBC and granule cell responses.

claim: Cre+ primary afferents contact granule cells and Golgi cells, but specifically target the ON subtype of UBCs.
source: These data indicate that Cre+ primary afferents contact granule cells and Golgi cells, but specifically target the ON subtype of UBCs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The principal neurons of MV project secondary vestibular afferents to lobe X.
source: A major target of the vestibular primary afferents is the medial vestibular nucleus of the brainstem (MV). The principal neurons of MV project secondary vestibular afferents to lobe X, and therefore represent a second potential source of mossy fiber input to UBCs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the vestibular circuit.

claim: Out of 108 UBCs recorded in brain slices from 14 mice, nine postsynaptic UBCs were of the OFF subtype.
source: Out of 108 UBCs recorded in brain slices from 14 mice, nine postsynaptic UBCs were of the OFF subtype: ChR2 activation of secondary afferents caused initial fast EPSCs that then depressed and led to a slow IPSC that caused a pause in spiking (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from electrophysiology experiments, supported by Figure 5B.

claim: In four additional cases, secondary vestibular afferents projected to ON UBCs.
source: In four additional cases, secondary vestibular afferents projected to ON UBCs, based on the presence of a slow inward current response (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from electrophysiology experiments, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: The fast EPSC amplitude correlated with the UBC brush area of OFF UBCs that received secondary input.
source: As was seen with ON UBCs that received primary input, the fast EPSC amplitude correlated with the UBC brush area of these OFF UBCs (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from correlation analysis, supported by Figure 5I.

claim: No correlations between the slow IPSC and mossy fiber-UBC contact area or UBC brush area were found for OFF UBCs.
source: No correlations between the slow IPSC and mossy fiber-UBC contact area or UBC brush area were found (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from correlation analysis, supported by Figure 5J.

claim: The EPSCs of secondary afferent-receiving ON UBCs were larger than those of secondary afferent-receiving OFF UBCs.
source: The EPSCs of secondary afferent-receiving ON UBCs were larger than those of secondary afferent-receiving OFF UBCs (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from electrophysiology experiments, supported by Figure 5K.

claim: EPSCs of ON UBCs that received secondary afferents were similar to ON UBCs that received primary afferents.
source: EPSCs of ON UBCs that received secondary afferents were similar to ON UBCs that received primary afferents (secondary: 45.17 ± 8.26 pA vs primary: 46.35 ± 14.09 pA, (mean ± sem), t-test, p=0.954, n = 11).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Of 231 mGluR1+ UBCs counted, 44 (19%) received labeled mossy fiber input from secondary afferents.
source: Of 231 mGluR1+ UBCs counted, 44 (19%) received labeled mossy fiber input.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from immunohistochemistry experiments.

claim: Of 114 calretinin+ UBCs counted, 19 (17%) received labeled mossy fiber input from secondary afferents.
source: Of 114 calretinin+ UBCs counted, 19 (17%) received labeled mossy fiber input.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from immunohistochemistry experiments.

claim: A similar proportion of mGluR1+ and calretinin+ UBCs are innervated by secondary afferents.
source: Thus, although their populations differ in number, a similar proportion of mGluR1+ and calretinin+ UBCs are innervated by secondary afferents.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the immunohistochemistry experiments.

claim: Primary and secondary afferents in the cerebellum appeared to have different morphologies.
source: Primary and secondary afferents in the cerebellum appeared to have different morphologies (Figure 6), suggesting that mossy fiber structure may differ depending upon their source.
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 6.

claim: Labeled secondary afferents were more numerous than primary afferents.
source: Labeled secondary afferents were more numerous than primary afferents (Figure 6A–B), although their number is somewhat artificial given the incomplete labeling of both VG and MV neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a caveat about incomplete labeling, supported by Figure 6A-B.

claim: Primary afferents only projected into IXc, whereas secondary afferents also projected into the more caudal lobe IXb.
source: Primary afferents only projected into IXc, whereas secondary afferents also projected into the more caudal lobe IXb (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 6C-D.

claim: The terminals of primary fibers were often 'rosette-like', similar to those of secondary afferents, but in many cases the elaborate protrusions from the main fiber ran along a longer length of the axon than the more spherically shaped secondary afferents.
source: The terminals of primary fibers were often 'rosette-like', similar to those of secondary afferents, but in many cases the elaborate protrusions from the main fiber ran along a longer length of the axon than the more spherically shaped secondary afferents (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 6E-F.

claim: Primary afferents were significantly thicker than secondary afferents.
source: Measurement of axon diameter between rosettes (mean of several measurements along axon >5 µm from mossy terminal swellings) indicated that primary afferents were significantly thicker than secondary afferents (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from morphological measurements, supported by Figure 6G.

claim: The UBCs that received secondary afferent input had larger dendritic brushes than UBCs that received primary input.
source: Surprisingly, the differences in morphology based on source of input also extended to the postsynaptic cells. The UBCs that received secondary afferent input had larger dendritic brushes than UBCs that received primary input.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from morphological measurements.

claim: In some cases, the primary-receiving UBC had a brush that wrapped around the primary afferent itself, rather than around an apparent swelling or rosette.
source: In some cases, the primary-receiving UBC had a brush that wrapped around the primary afferent itself, rather than around an apparent swelling or rosette (Figure 7A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that release sites can be located at these regions of the axon.
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 7A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Release sites can be located at regions of the axon that are not apparent swellings or rosettes.
source: In some cases, the primary-receiving UBC had a brush that wrapped around the primary afferent itself, rather than around an apparent swelling or rosette (Figure 7A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that release sites can be located at these regions of the axon.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the observation of brushes wrapping around smooth axon regions, supported by Figure 7A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Secondary-receiving UBCs were more likely to contact a spherically shaped rosette.
source: Secondary-receiving UBCs were more likely to contact a spherically shaped rosette (Figure 7B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 7B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The contact area between primary afferents and UBCs was smaller than the contact area between secondary afferents and UBCs.
source: Measurements of the contact area between afferent and UBC, indicated that the area between primary afferents and UBCs was smaller than the contact area between secondary afferents and UBCs, likely due to the more complex rosettes made by secondary afferents (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from morphological measurements, supported by Figure 7C.

claim: The smaller contact area between primary afferents and UBCs is likely due to the more complex rosettes made by secondary afferents.
source: Measurements of the contact area between afferent and UBC, indicated that the area between primary afferents and UBCs was smaller than the contact area between secondary afferents and UBCs, likely due to the more complex rosettes made by secondary afferents (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the morphological observations, supported by Figure 7C.

claim: The dendritic brush of secondary-receiving UBCs was larger in area and volume than the brushes of primary-receiving UBCs.
source: Even the dendritic brush (including non-synaptic membrane) of secondary-receiving UBCs was larger in area and volume than the brushes of primary-receiving UBCs (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from morphological measurements, supported by Figure 7D.

claim: The secondary-afferent receiving ON UBCs were similar in size to the secondary-receiving OFF UBCs.
source: These differences were not due to OFF UBCs being larger than ON UBCs, because the secondary-afferent receiving ON UBCs were similar in size to the secondary-receiving OFF UBCs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from morphological measurements.

claim: The contact area between the brush and mossy fiber relative to the entire surface area of the brush was similar between primary and secondary-receiving UBCs.
source: The contact area between the brush and mossy fiber relative to the entire surface area of the brush was similar between primary and secondary-receiving UBCs (t-test, p=0.180, n = 17).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from morphological measurements.

claim: The postsynaptic brush develops in such a way to match the anatomy of the earlier maturing mossy fiber.
source: This suggests that the postsynaptic brush develops in such a way to match the anatomy of the earlier maturing mossy fiber (Ashwell and Zhang, 1998; Sekerková et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with citations to Ashwell and Zhang, 1998; Sekerková et al., 2004.

claim: UBCs targeted by primary and secondary afferents differed in soma size, regardless of ON/OFF subtype.
source: Finally, UBCs targeted by primary and secondary afferents even differed in soma size, regardless of ON/OFF subtype (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from morphological measurements, supported by Figure 7E.

claim: The global morphology of UBCs is tuned to the source of mossy fiber.
source: Thus, the global morphology of UBCs is tuned to the source of mossy fiber.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the morphological measurements.

claim: Build-up EPSCs are AMPAR-mediated.
source: These AMPAR-mediated EPSCs are distinct from typical synaptic responses due to their slow activation during the stimulus and slow decay upon cessation of stimulation and their lack of fast EPSCs; notably, they lacked the slow inward current that appears only after transmission ceases, characteristic of the ON UBC.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of build-up EPSCs.

claim: Build-up EPSCs are distinct from typical synaptic responses due to their slow activation during the stimulus and slow decay upon cessation of stimulation and their lack of fast EPSCs.
source: These AMPAR-mediated EPSCs are distinct from typical synaptic responses due to their slow activation during the stimulus and slow decay upon cessation of stimulation and their lack of fast EPSCs; notably, they lacked the slow inward current that appears only after transmission ceases, characteristic of the ON UBC.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of build-up EPSCs.

claim: Build-up EPSCs lacked the slow inward current that appears only after transmission ceases, characteristic of the ON UBC.
source: These AMPAR-mediated EPSCs are distinct from typical synaptic responses due to their slow activation during the stimulus and slow decay upon cessation of stimulation and their lack of fast EPSCs; notably, they lacked the slow inward current that appears only after transmission ceases, characteristic of the ON UBC.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of build-up EPSCs.

claim: Build-up responses were previously considered to arise from variation in apposition of receptors and release sites at mossy fiber terminals.
source: Previously these build-up responses were considered to arise from variation in apposition of receptors and release sites at mossy fiber terminals (Zampini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Zampini et al., 2016.

claim: Build-up EPSCs were small with a 6.06 ± 2.05 pA (mean ± SD) peak in response to ten stimuli at 50 Hz.
source: ChR2-evoked build-up EPSCs were small (Figure 8A), with a 6.06 ± 2.05 pA (mean ± SD) peak in response to ten stimuli at 50 Hz, and had a decay time constant of 445.38 ± 302.43 ms (n = 5 UBCs).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from electrophysiology experiments, supported by Figure 8A.

claim: Build-up EPSCs had a decay time constant of 445.38 ± 302.43 ms (n = 5 UBCs).
source: ChR2-evoked build-up EPSCs were small (Figure 8A), with a 6.06 ± 2.05 pA (mean ± SD) peak in response to ten stimuli at 50 Hz, and had a decay time constant of 445.38 ± 302.43 ms (n = 5 UBCs).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from electrophysiology experiments, supported by Figure 8A.

claim: In all four cases in which build-up EPSCs were evoked by primary afferent optogenetic activation and the UBC was recovered, there was no mossy fiber contact to the UBC brush.
source: In all four cases in which build-up EPSCs were evoked by primary afferent optogenetic activation and the UBC was recovered, there was no mossy fiber contact to the UBC brush (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from electrophysiology and morphology experiments, supported by Figure 8C-D.

claim: In all cases of build-up EPSCs, primary afferents contacted UBC somata.
source: Rather, in all of these cases, primary afferents contacted UBC somata.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from morphology experiments.

claim: In all cases of recovered UBCs that did not have apparent build-up EPSCs, none had a ChR2-expressing mossy fiber contacting the soma.
source: Additionally, in all cases of recovered UBCs that did not have apparent build-up EPSCs, none had a ChR2-expressing mossy fiber contacting the soma (n = 5 primary-receiving UBCs) (cf. Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from electrophysiology and morphology experiments, supported by Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The build-up response represents activity of an unconventional UBC input, but generated by a primary afferent.
source: Thus, the build-up response represents activity of an unconventional UBC input, but generated by a primary afferent.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the electrophysiology and morphology experiments.

claim: A UBC receiving both contact to the brush and to the soma would be predicted to have a typical ON UBC response (due to the brush contact) with an additional build-up EPSC (due to the soma contact).
source: If the build-up response is due to somatic synapses, then a UBC receiving both contact to the brush and to the soma would be predicted to have a typical ON UBC response (due to the brush contact) with an additional build-up EPSC (due to the soma contact).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on the hypothesis that build-up responses are due to somatic synapses.

claim: In a primary-receiving ON UBC that had contact with the same mossy fiber on both the brush and the soma, the ChR2-evoked response was a combination of the typical fast EPSC plus a build-up EPSC.
source: Indeed, in a primary-receiving ON UBC that had contact with the same mossy fiber on both the brush and the soma, the ChR2-evoked response was a combination of the typical fast EPSC plus a build-up EPSC (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from electrophysiology and morphology experiments, supported by Figure 8E.

claim: Shank1 confirmed that postsynaptic receptors may be present at the somatic membrane in regions that appear to contact the primary afferent.
source: Shank1, a postsynaptic density protein, confirmed that postsynaptic receptors may be present at the somatic membrane in regions that appear to contact the primary afferent (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from immunohistochemistry experiments, supported by Figure 8E.

claim: In no case did electrical stimulation evoke an OFF UBC response in UBCs with build-up responses, and thus it may be that axosomatic synapses are only made onto ON UBCs.
source: In no case did electrical stimulation evoke an OFF UBC response, and thus it may be that axosomatic synapses are only made onto ON UBCs.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The vestibular cerebellum is unique in its high density of UBCs.
source: The vestibular cerebellum is unique in its high density of UBCs, suggesting a cerebellar processing function of UBCs specific to the vestibular system.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: The high density of UBCs in vestibular cerebellum suggests a cerebellar processing function of UBCs specific to the vestibular system.
source: The vestibular cerebellum is unique in its high density of UBCs, suggesting a cerebellar processing function of UBCs specific to the vestibular system.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the high density of UBCs in vestibular cerebellum.

claim: Different cerebellar input pathways differentially recruit ON and OFF UBC response classes based on extraordinary specificity of innervation.
source: This study demonstrates that different cerebellar input pathways differentially recruit these response classes based on extraordinary specificity of innervation (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings, supported by Figure 9.

claim: ON and OFF cells are co-distributed in lobe X.
source: Although ON and OFF cells are co-distributed in lobe X, primary afferents project to ON UBCs exclusively.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the discussion.

claim: Primary afferents that project to ON UBCs are specifically the fibers of VG neurons whose peripheral endings are largely in the semicircular canals, and make both calyx and bouton endings (dimorphic VG fibers).
source: These primary afferents specifically are the fibers of VG neurons whose peripheral endings are largely in the semicircular canals, and make both calyx and bouton endings (dimorphic VG fibers).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings in the discussion.

claim: UBCs act as an input layer prior to the granule cells to allow divergence to parallel ensembles of postsynaptic granule cells that each faithfully represent head movement along the axes of different end organs.
source: Instead, UBCs could act as an input layer prior to the granule cells to allow divergence to parallel ensembles of postsynaptic granule cells that each faithfully represent head movement along the axes of different end organs.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the discussion.

claim: Convergence of signals from the canals and otoliths must occur at some point to integrate signals, which is necessary to estimate orientation relative to gravity.
source: Convergence must occur at some point to integrate signals from the canals and otoliths, which is necessary to estimate orientation relative to gravity, and this may happen at the granule cell and/or Purkinje cell level.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the discussion.

claim: Convergence of vestibular signals may happen at the granule cell and/or Purkinje cell level.
source: Convergence must occur at some point to integrate signals from the canals and otoliths, which is necessary to estimate orientation relative to gravity, and this may happen at the granule cell and/or Purkinje cell level.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the discussion.

claim: Convergence occurring in the MV could be processed specifically by UBCs that receive secondary input.
source: Alternatively, or in addition, convergence occurring in the MV could be processed specifically by UBCs that receive secondary input.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the discussion.

claim: MV neurons receive multiple primary afferent inputs.
source: MV neurons receive multiple primary afferent inputs, feedback inhibition from Purkinje cells, and can be inhibited by stimulation of the contralateral vestibular organs (Shimazu and Precht, 1966; Uchino et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Shimazu and Precht, 1966; Uchino et al., 1986.

claim: MV neurons receive feedback inhibition from Purkinje cells.
source: MV neurons receive multiple primary afferent inputs, feedback inhibition from Purkinje cells, and can be inhibited by stimulation of the contralateral vestibular organs (Shimazu and Precht, 1966; Uchino et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Shimazu and Precht, 1966; Uchino et al., 1986.

claim: MV neurons can be inhibited by stimulation of the contralateral vestibular organs.
source: MV neurons receive multiple primary afferent inputs, feedback inhibition from Purkinje cells, and can be inhibited by stimulation of the contralateral vestibular organs (Shimazu and Precht, 1966; Uchino et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Shimazu and Precht, 1966; Uchino et al., 1986.

claim: Secondary vestibular mossy fibers may carry signals integrated from multiple end organs and both hemispheres to both ON and OFF UBCs.
source: Thus, secondary vestibular mossy fibers may carry signals integrated from multiple end organs and both hemispheres to both ON and OFF UBCs.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the connectivity of MV neurons.

claim: OFF UBCs process bilateral vestibular signals to pause input to ensembles of granule cells, perhaps in a push-pull circuit that could contribute to reflexive eye movements.
source: This circuitry indicates that OFF UBCs process bilateral vestibular signals to pause input to ensembles of granule cells, perhaps in a push-pull circuit that could contribute to reflexive eye movements.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the discussion.

claim: MV neurons respond to synaptic input with high-fidelity EPSCs whose amplitudes are rate-invariant.
source: The rate of input to secondary afferent-receiving UBCs may be preserved by MV neurons, which are known to respond to synaptic input with high-fidelity EPSCs whose amplitudes are rate-invariant (McElvain et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to McElvain et al., 2015.

claim: Granule cells respond faithfully to mossy fiber input in vivo, responding to a burst of mossy fiber input with a burst of action potentials that is similar in duration.
source: In addition, granule cells respond faithfully to mossy fiber input in vivo, responding to a burst of mossy fiber input with a burst of action potentials that is similar in duration (Arenz et al., 2008; Chadderton et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Arenz et al., 2008; Chadderton et al., 2004.

claim: Profound signal processing occurs at UBCs through highly rate-dependent EPSC amplitudes and long duration responses that may even be inverted by OFF UBCs.
source: It is at UBCs where profound signal processing occurs through highly rate-dependent EPSC amplitudes and long duration responses that may even be inverted by OFF UBCs (Kennedy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Kennedy et al., 2014.

claim: A longer duration burst of action potentials conveyed to the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapse will be more likely to drive the Purkinje cell because of facilitation at this synapse.
source: This extended response could be particularly important in the cerebellum. A longer duration burst of action potentials conveyed to the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapse will be more likely to drive the Purkinje cell because of facilitation at this synapse and would extend the window of integration within which climbing fiber activity can influence circuit learning.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about the functional significance of extended UBC responses.

claim: Extended UBC responses would extend the window of integration within which climbing fiber activity can influence circuit learning.
source: This extended response could be particularly important in the cerebellum. A longer duration burst of action potentials conveyed to the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapse will be more likely to drive the Purkinje cell because of facilitation at this synapse and would extend the window of integration within which climbing fiber activity can influence circuit learning.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about the functional significance of extended UBC responses.

claim: It is likely that a single granule cell integrates both primary and secondary inputs but also intrinsic mossy fiber input from UBCs.
source: At the level of the vestibular granule cell, it is likely that a single neuron integrates both primary and secondary inputs (Chabrol et al., 2015) but also intrinsic mossy fiber input from UBCs.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with citation to Chabrol et al., 2015.

claim: Mossy fibers from different sources may exhibit different forms of short-term plasticity.
source: (Chabrol et al., 2015) emphasized that mossy fibers from different sources may exhibit different forms of short-term plasticity, and these characteristic time-dependent responses impact the integrative function of the granule cell.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Chabrol et al., 2015.

claim: Characteristic time-dependent responses of mossy fibers impact the integrative function of the granule cell.
source: (Chabrol et al., 2015) emphasized that mossy fibers from different sources may exhibit different forms of short-term plasticity, and these characteristic time-dependent responses impact the integrative function of the granule cell.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Chabrol et al., 2015.

claim: Granule cells that receive some dendritic input from a UBC's intrinsic mossy fiber likely will be dominated by that input while the UBC is active.
source: Given the radical transformation of mossy fiber input by UBCs, which results in prolonged or delayed firing, or cessation in activity in vivo (Kennedy et al., 2014), granule cells that receive some dendritic input from a UBC's intrinsic mossy fiber likely will be dominated by that input while the UBC is active.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with citation to Kennedy et al., 2014.

claim: Brodal and Drablos (1963) suggested that vestibular lobes of rat cerebellum contain a population of mossy fibers that differ from those of other lobes.
source: Brodal and Drablos (1963) suggested that vestibular lobes of rat cerebellum contain a population of mossy fibers that differ from those of other lobes.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Brodal and Drablos, 1963.

claim: The fibers reported by Brodal and Drablos may have been intrinsic mossy fibers of UBCs.
source: The fact that they reported these fibers in flocculus, despite a dearth of primary afferents (Newlands and Perachio, 2003; Osanai et al., 1999), implies that these fibers may have been intrinsic mossy fibers of UBCs, as suggested by Rossi et al. (1995).
evidence: This is stated as an inference with citations to Newlands and Perachio, 2003; Osanai et al., 1999; Rossi et al., 1995.

claim: Differences in morphology between mossy fibers based on their source have been reported in non-vestibular lobes of the cerebellum.
source: Differences in morphology between mossy fibers based on their source have been reported in non-vestibular lobes of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: Mossy fibers projecting from the deep cerebellar nuclei are larger, are more likely to have filipodia projecting from the rosette, and have more boutons, than those projecting from basal pontine nuclei.
source: Mossy fibers projecting from the deep cerebellar nuclei are larger, are more likely to have filipodia projecting from the rosette, and have more boutons, than those projecting from basal pontine nuclei (Gao et al., 2016; Gilmer and Person, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Gao et al., 2016; Gilmer and Person, 2017.

claim: Mossy fibers originating from different regions that project to lobe X vary in presynaptic plasticity.
source: While mossy fibers originating from different regions that project to lobe X vary in presynaptic plasticity (Chabrol et al., 2015), we find that these axons also exhibit characteristic morphological features that may support differences in electrical activity level.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Chabrol et al., 2015.

claim: The characteristic morphological features of mossy fibers may support differences in electrical activity level.
source: While mossy fibers originating from different regions that project to lobe X vary in presynaptic plasticity (Chabrol et al., 2015), we find that these axons also exhibit characteristic morphological features that may support differences in electrical activity level.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the discussion.

claim: The diameter of primary vestibular afferents in the vestibular nerve is among the thickest in the brain (mean, ~3 µm).
source: It is perhaps not surprising that the primary vestibular afferents in the cerebellum are large given that their diameter in the vestibular nerve is among the thickest in the brain (mean, ~3 µm) (Gacek and Rasmussen, 1961); notably, these also have elevated tonic firing rates of >100 Hz (Jones et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Gacek and Rasmussen, 1961.

claim: Primary vestibular afferents have elevated tonic firing rates of >100 Hz.
source: It is perhaps not surprising that the primary vestibular afferents in the cerebellum are large given that their diameter in the vestibular nerve is among the thickest in the brain (mean, ~3 µm) (Gacek and Rasmussen, 1961); notably, these also have elevated tonic firing rates of >100 Hz (Jones et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Jones et al., 2008.

claim: The relatively thin diameter of the secondary afferents suggests lower firing rates.
source: The relatively thin diameter of the secondary afferents suggests lower firing rates (Perge et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as an inference with citation to Perge et al., 2012.

claim: Vestibular nucleus neurons that respond to vestibular stimulation in vivo have spontaneous firing rates between 0 and 30 Hz in cats and ~65 Hz in squirrel monkeys.
source: Indeed, vestibular nucleus neurons that respond to vestibular stimulation in vivo have spontaneous firing rates between 0 and 30 Hz in cats and ~65 Hz in squirrel monkeys (Cullen and McCrea, 1993; Shimazu and Precht, 1965).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Cullen and McCrea, 1993; Shimazu and Precht, 1965.

claim: EPSCs recorded in granule cells in the flocculus occurred at ~13 Hz under anesthesia.
source: In mice, the best approximation of spontaneous firing of secondary mossy fibers may be the EPSCs recorded in granule cells in the flocculus that could be modulated by vestibular stimulation. These EPSCs occurred at ~13 Hz under anesthesia (Arenz et al., 2008), much lower than vestibular nerve fibers.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Arenz et al., 2008.

claim: Smooth parts of the primary afferent contacting a UBC soma could evoke EPSCs.
source: This is corroborated by the finding that smooth parts of the primary afferent contacting a UBC soma could evoke EPSCs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Differences in en passant mossy terminal morphology might affect efficiency of propagating action potentials.
source: Such differences in en passant mossy terminal morphology might affect efficiency of propagating action potentials.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the discussion.

claim: Previous descriptions of build-up responses in UBCs speculated that such responses might arise from misalignment of a mossy fiber active zone relative to an AMPAR cluster.
source: Previous descriptions of build-up responses in UBCs speculated that such responses might arise from misalignment of a mossy fiber active zone relative to an AMPAR cluster (Zampini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Zampini et al., 2016.

claim: The observation that build-up EPSCs occur specifically when mossy fibers appear to contact UBC somas demonstrates a novel basis for these synaptic currents.
source: Instead, the observation that build-up EPSCs occur specifically when mossy fibers appear to contact UBC somas demonstrates a novel basis for these synaptic currents.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the electrophysiology and morphology experiments.

claim: UBC somata express some AMPA receptors sufficient to respond to somatic inputs.
source: Apparently, UBC somata express some AMPA receptors sufficient to respond to somatic inputs. Indeed, outside-out patch-clamp recording has previously shown that AMPARs do function in somatic membranes of UBCs (Kinney et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Kinney et al., 1997.

claim: Previous analysis of electron micrographs highlighted mossy fiber terminals that contacted Golgi cell somata, forming large convoluted 'en marron' synapses.
source: Previous analysis of electron micrographs highlighted mossy fiber terminals that contacted Golgi cell somata, forming large convoluted 'en marron' synapses (Chan-Palay and Palay, 1971), which are distinct from the club-like endings contacting UBCs.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Chan-Palay and Palay, 1971.

claim: Mossy fibers touching granule cell somata have been observed, although these same mossy fibers only made definitive synaptic contacts with nearby granule cell dendrites.
source: Mossy fibers touching granule cell somata have also been observed, although these same mossy fibers only made definitive synaptic contacts with nearby granule cell dendrites (Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974.

claim: Somatic contacts by mossy fibers associated with distinct postsynaptic responses suggests that somatic inputs could represent a previously unappreciated form of transmission in the granule region of the cerebellum.
source: The fortuitous observation of somatic contacts by mossy fibers that were associated with distinct postsynaptic responses suggests that somatic inputs could represent a previously unappreciated form of transmission in the granule region of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the findings on build-up responses and somatic contacts.
